name: App architecture
routing_text: Structuring an application codebase: modular monoliths versus microservices, module and service boundaries, vertical slices, hexagonal ports and adapters, clean and onion architecture, domain driven design, coupling and cohesion, encapsulation, and keeping business logic out of the web framework.
blurb: How to cut an application into modules that survive contact with a team.

units.title: microservices, module, modules, monolith, modularity, component
units.summary: A good monolith is a monolith that is easy to change, easy to modify, and easy to extend. Slices of functionality ensure exactly one request going in and one response coming out, with all logic in a single action class. Using microservices can make a system easier while the performance gets worse. Microservices are supposed to be independently deployable, unlike modules in a monolith, which are all deployed together in a single monolithic deployment.

units.title: hexagonal architecture, layered architecture, ports and adapters, business logic, domain, place order
units.summary: Slicing your ports and adapters code into multiple source trees can stop infrastructure code from talking to each other at compile time. You could opt to remove the quantity check at the API level because it is also handled by the Pydantic model. The payments area should have a primary port. The SQLAlchemy inventory adapter gets the connection.

units.title: coupling, codebase, system, cohesion, intrusive coupling, distance
units.summary: When we design software and create structures in our code bases, we create a formalized bet on the changes we are going to see in the future. Structured design was introduced in the 1960s and proposed six coupling levels: content, common, external, control, stamp, and data coupling. A change that touches a request means the service class must be adapted and a new field added to the database, coupling all that code. Coupling was introduced in the late 1960s, and connascence in the 1990s, creating a 30-year cadence.

units.title: database, sharding, shard, cache, caching, partitioning
units.summary: Every time a queue is created, information about it is stored in the database. It is possible to refactor the database to break dependencies down at the lowest database level. User feedback starts to collect into a dataset. Horizontal partitioning operates at row level or document level.

rubrics.criterion: Keep transport and persistence concerns out of domain logic.
rubrics.check: Scan the domain/business layer for imports or calls to the web framework, HTTP exceptions, API request/response types, and database connection or session types; fail on any occurrence.
rubrics.why: Mixing those concerns with domain logic couples the business to I/O, makes unit tests need mocks, and replaces domain language with transport details.
rubrics.unit_title: microservices, module, modules, monolith, modularity, component

rubrics.criterion: Make each module independently changeable: a change inside a module must not force changes in other modules.
rubrics.check: Draw the module dependency graph; fail on cycles, references into another module's internals, or commits where one logical change edits files across module boundaries.
rubrics.why: When every change touches multiple modules, work becomes about not breaking the rest of the application instead of coding the feature.
rubrics.unit_title: microservices, module, modules, monolith, modularity, component

rubrics.criterion: Do not claim 'modular' until explicit module boundaries exist.
rubrics.check: Look for enforced boundary rules: separate modules with public APIs, dependency constraints, or architecture tests; if none are present, fail the modularity claim.
rubrics.why: Renaming a monolith or microservices that are already a mess does not fix it; without boundaries the same tangled structure continues under a new label.

rubrics.criterion: Give every named component in your architecture diagrams or descriptions an explicit structural counterpart in the code.
rubrics.check: For each component box in a component-level diagram or named subsystem in docs, locate a package, module or class with a matching name; if a component is only a conceptual grouping of classes spread across layers, fail.
rubrics.why: When the documented structure does not exist in code, the diagrams stop reflecting the implementation and the mental model breaks.

rubrics.criterion: Isolate domain and business logic from transport, HTTP and persistence framework concerns.
rubrics.check: In every unit that contains business rules, look for imports of web/HTTP frameworks, HTTP exceptions, database connections/session parameters, and response-shaped return types; any occurrence inside the domain layer fails.
rubrics.why: If business logic depends on a database or HTTP, tests need mock infrastructure and a domain concept cannot be expressed in its own language; changing persistence or transport framework forces changes to business code.
rubrics.unit_title: hexagonal architecture, layered architecture, ports and adapters, business logic, domain, place order

rubrics.criterion: Keep different modules or bounded contexts on separate data models and schemas.
rubrics.check: Find each relational table/collection or entity class shared by two modules, services or bounded contexts; if two units read/write the same table or one data model serves multiple business domains, fail.
rubrics.why: Shared schemas couple all consumers to one representation, so a change to one domain's data or rules requires hunting across every place that uses that model.
rubrics.unit_title: hexagonal architecture, layered architecture, ports and adapters, business logic, domain, place order

rubrics.criterion: Give every functional area an explicit boundary, and group code for that area in one feature package rather than spreading it across technical layers.
rubrics.check: Pick one feature, for example orders. Look at the top-level package or directory structure. If the feature's code is split across packages named web, business/domain and data, or if different features share the same area with no boundary, fail.
rubrics.why: Without boundaries around functional areas, business areas compete in the same change surface; vertical feature slices make the feature cohesive and findable in one place.
rubrics.unit_title: coupling, codebase, system, cohesion, intrusive coupling, distance

rubrics.criterion: Before calling a module independent, count its incoming and outgoing dependencies instead of judging it by size.
rubrics.check: Generate a dependency graph for the modules. For each module, count the modules it depends on and the modules that depend on it. A module with many arrows in either direction is not independent, no matter how small it is.
rubrics.why: Small boundaries by themselves only distribute coupled code; independence is determined by dependency arrows, and reducing those arrows is what decouples modules.
rubrics.unit_title: coupling, codebase, system, cohesion, intrusive coupling, distance

evidence.quote: measure the independence of a given module by counting how many modules does it depend on and then how many modules depend on it

rubrics.criterion: Add fitness functions to the build that assert limits on coupling and cyclomatic complexity.
rubrics.check: Look in the build/CI configuration and repository for automated architecture checks or fitness functions that assert coupling or cyclomatic complexity. If none exist, fail.
rubrics.why: Without automated assertions, sprint-driven shortcuts erode the codebase until a refactoring sprint is needed; fitness functions make structural quality checks part of every build.
rubrics.unit_title: coupling, codebase, system, cohesion, intrusive coupling, distance

rubrics.criterion: Hide database access behind a dedicated facade or port so business logic does not execute SQL or depend on a database library.
rubrics.check: Open the endpoint/handler and service classes; mark fail if you find SQL, ORM calls, or the database library imported in the business layer; pass if all data access goes through a named facade/service.
rubrics.why: Direct database integration couples the domain to infrastructure and turns it into a complete mess.
